story: The Mole Creek area sits on limestone that in places is up to two kilometres thick. Water seeping through it has dissolved some of the largest and deepest caves in Australia, along with sinkholes, gorges and springs, an internationally significant karst system. Numerous caves lie in the park; only two are open to the public, and the rest are the domain of recreational cavers, for whom Mole Creek is a mecca.

Life in the caves runs on what streams carry in. Insects and plant material washed into Marakoopa Cave feed a food web of animals adapted to total darkness; those that never leave the caves, the troglobites, have no need of eyes and find their way with long feelers. Cockerill's cave beetle, the cave harvestman Hickmanoxyomma gibbergunyar and the extremely rare cave false scorpion are found nowhere but this park. The glow-worms of Marakoopa are the larvae of a mosquito-like fly whose light comes from a chemical reaction in its body.

Historical records suggest that the Mole Creek region lay in the territory of the Northern nation of Aboriginal people. They gathered ochre from mines at Mount Vandyke and the Gog Range, Toolumbunner, travelling by well-kept tracks held open by burning; a major route ran east to west between Quamby Bluff and Mount Vandyke. Aboriginal cultural heritage in Tasmania is a living, spiritual connection for Tasmanian Aboriginal people today.

The first Europeans to find the karst were Van Diemen's Land Company surveyors seeking a rail route to the west coast in the 1830s. A paling splitter stumbled on King Solomons Cave in 1906, and by 1912 Marakoopa Cave was open to the public. In the 1920s the state's Tourism Department bought land around the cave entrances. The national park was declared in 1996 to protect some of the finest and most visited cave systems in Tasmania, and today lies within the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area.
howItWorks: Mole Creek Karst is managed by the Tasmania Parks and Wildlife Service (PWS), and the park works a little differently from the others: you do not need a parks pass to tour the show caves, but you do need one to explore other parts of the park, such as the picnic ground and forest walks at Croesus Reserve on the Mersey. Entry to the caves is by guided tour only.

Tours run every day except Christmas Day and last 45 minutes. Group sizes are capped, so book ahead by phone up to 14 days before your visit; large groups must book. Tickets for both caves are sold at the central office at 330 Mayberry Road, about 600 metres before the Marakoopa entrance. At Marakoopa there is a choice of the easy Underground Rivers and Glow Worms tour or the Great Cathedral and Glow Worms tour, which needs medium fitness to climb the stairway.

Tripods, food and drink are not allowed in the caves. Photography, including flash, is allowed except in the glow-worm chamber. PWS lists the park as a Fuel Stove Only Area, and dogs and recreational drones are not allowed.

sightNotes.poi-au-mole-creek-karst-marakoopa-cave: Two streams run through this cave of crystals, reflective pools and stalactites. The Great Cathedral chamber amplifies voices, and its glow-worm display is Australia's largest in a public cave.
sightNotes.poi-au-mole-creek-karst-king-solomons-ca: A compact, drier cave found by a paling splitter in 1906, lavishly decorated with sparkling calcite, shawls, stalactites and stalagmites. Suitable for all ages.

chronology.text: Northern nation people quarry ochre at Mount Vandyke and the Gog Range (Toolumbunner), travelling on tracks kept open by fire.
Van Diemen's Land Company surveyors seeking a rail route west are the first Europeans to find the karst.
A paling splitter stumbles across King Solomons Cave.
Marakoopa Cave is open to the public.
The Tourism Department buys land beside the cave entrances to develop them for visitors.
Mole Creek Karst National Park is declared to protect the caves.

safety: The caves are a steady 9°C: dress warmly and wear walking shoes for stairs and uneven, sometimes narrow passages.

The cave tours are not suitable for most people with impaired mobility, because of steps, uneven surfaces, low ceilings and narrow sections; accessible picnic tables and toilets are near the Marakoopa car park.
The Great Cathedral tour climbs a stairway and needs medium fitness; the Underground Rivers and King Solomons tours suit all ages.
regulations: Entry to the show caves is by guided tour only.
No tripods, food or drink in the caves, and no photography in the Marakoopa glow-worm chamber.
Fuel Stove Only Area: fires are prohibited.
Dogs and recreational drones are not allowed in Tasmanian national parks.

weather: Underground the weather never changes: both caves stay at a cool 9°C all year, so bring a warm layer even on a hot summer day, and wear walking shoes for the stairs. Outside, the park lies on the slopes of the Great Western Tiers in northern Tasmania, and Tasmanian weather can change quickly at any time of year. Because the tours run daily in every season, the caves are a good choice when rain or snow makes the mountain walks unappealing; the extra afternoon tours from October to April suit long summer days.
directions: The park is about 40 minutes west of Deloraine. Take the B12 from Deloraine through Mole Creek. The first signposted turn-off leads to the ticket office and Marakoopa Cave at 330 Mayberry Road, Mayberry; the second, a further 7 kilometres along the B12, leads to King Solomons Cave at 1535 Liena Road, Liena. Allow at least 15 minutes to drive between the two caves. Parking at the upper Marakoopa car park is limited and the road is narrow: motor homes, caravans and camper trailers must stay at the lower car park by the ticket office, a 10- to 15-minute walk from the cave. The drive through Chudleigh, Mole Creek and Caveside is scenic in its own right.
